en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra titled "The Noble Exposition of the Miraculous Manifestations of the Empowerment of the Buddha's Powers.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Blessed One was seated on the bank of the great river Nairañjanā together with seven thousand bodhisattvas headed by the noble Avalokiteśvara, Vajrapāṇi, Maitreya, and Mañjuśrī;

and together with all the great śrāvakas headed by Subhūti, Śāriputra, and Maudgalyāyana; and he was honored, revered, and worshipped by Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders.
Having finished his meal, the Blessed One sat down in the circle of the assembly and gladdened, exhorted, inspired, and delighted them with a discourse connected with the Dharma.
Then the Tathāgata, having gone from the city of Maharddhi to Vārāṇasī, sat down in the Āmrapālī grove within that circle of the assembly.
At that time, the great earth trembled and shook violently.

There stood a single great lion-throne made of various jewels, fashioned from the seven precious substances, one *yojana* in height and half a *yojana* in width. It was well-cushioned, exceedingly delightful, charming, strewn with divine cloths, hung with various divine flowers and fruits, and endowed with divine fragrance and color.
Upon beholding the roots of merit planted by the Tathāgatas, all sentient beings attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Then the Blessed One, seated upon the lion throne, attained the samādhi named *Buddhāvataṃsaka*.
Then, having arisen from that samādhi, he addressed the noble Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi as follows:

"Avalokiteśvara, go to the great world-system and, throughout the world-systems in the ten directions, [teach] those beings who are to be disciplined—those who are possessed of the five degenerations, who lack faith, who engage in evil conduct, who are shrouded by afflictions, and who do not honor their mothers or fathers."

"O Vajrapāṇi, you two, having attained great supernatural power and the strength of meditative concentration, must gather and collect all those who are not true ascetics, not true brahmins, and who lack faith in the Three Jewels, by condensing them into this garland of maṇḍalas. Then,
having heard the words of the Tathāgata and having looked upon all sentient beings, the noble Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi entered the meditative concentration named "Arousal."

By the power of that samādhi, the great earth shook, trembled, and quaked in six ways. From the Brahma-world within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, up to the realm of form, the radiance of their two bodies appeared. Then, from that radiance, these verses of exhortation issued forth:
Then, at the conclusion of the verses issued from the radiance of his body, every single being throughout the entire trichiliocosm was informed and inspired by this succession.
All those beings abandoned false views and became endowed with right view. Those who were possessed of pride, intoxication, and arrogance became free from pride, intoxication, and arrogance.

Those who had followed after sensual desire and were heedless—those engaged in killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and the other eight unwholesome dharmas—were turned away from them and established upon the Noble Eightfold Path.

Having all abandoned restlessness, laughter, dance, play, greed, anger, envy, passion, and so forth, they became desirous of seeing, attending upon, serving, and hearing the Dharma from the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata was honored by the kings of the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, garuḍas, and mahoragas, as well as by their ministers, and by the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, with all kinds of divine flowers, garlands, perfumes, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and so forth. Then they all approached the Āmrapālī grove in the great city of Vārāṇasī, and through the power of the merit and roots of goodness planted by the Tathāgatas, they rained down a shower of flowers upon the Tathāgata.

Then, at that time, the Blessed One established the Āmrapālī grove in Jambudvīpa as extending for hundreds of thousands of millions of *yojanas* all around, level like the palm of a hand, divine, delightful, and endowed with exquisite color.

It was adorned with celestial flower-trees, fragrance-trees, fruit-trees, great jewel-trees, wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), clothing-trees, and so forth; it was furnished with celestial seats and illuminated by garlands of precious cloth, and was golden in hue.

Adorned with the sound of divine strings of tinkling bells— just like the world-system Sukhāvatī— it was so pleasing, refreshing, lovely, and delightful that it was filled with all the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, laymen, laywomen, kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders, and he established himself therein.
Then the Bodhisattva Āryāvalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi, having arisen from that samādhi, approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and circumambulated him three times to the right, they said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, the Tathāgatas possess skillful means for the sake of maturing sentient beings."

"O Blessed One, many bodhisattvas, great śrāvakas, kings, ministers, householders, and citizens among the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, as well as monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen,
have assembled here through the splendor of the Tathāgata and by the power of his miraculous transformations.
Excellent, excellent, noble sons!"

In the same way, O sons of the Conqueror, many Tathāgatas, having understood the conduct of sentient beings—whose intentions are diverse, who have attained various roots of merit according to what is needed for their discipline, and whose inclinations are manifold—teach the Dharma as a skillful means for the sake of maturing sentient beings.

Some sentient beings are to be disciplined by Bodhisattvas; some are to be disciplined by Śrāvakas; some are to be disciplined by Pratyekabuddhas; some are to be disciplined by gods; some are to be disciplined by Śakra; and some are to be disciplined by Brahmā.

Some are to be converted by nāgas; some by those possessing great supernatural powers (mahardhika); some by kings; some by meditative concentration (samādhi); some by hearing the Dharma; some by miracles (prātihārya); some by the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata; some by relics (dhātu).

Some are eager for conversion through the roots of merit arising from the construction of caityas, the building of monasteries, walkways, and gardens; some are to be converted through the roots of merit arising from the commissioning of stone images, paintings, and images made of gold, silver, or bronze.

Some are disciples eager for the roots of merit consisting in honoring and revering the community of monks; some are disciples eager for the roots of merit consisting in inquiring about, writing, reciting, and honoring the sūtras; some are eager for lamps, flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, food, and ornaments.
They are not endowed with the roots of merit of the ultimate truth, nor are they endowed with the qualities of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, O sons of the Conqueror, regarding all phenomena, there is nothing for the Tathāgatas that is unknown, unseen, unheard, or unperceived.
They know what has come to pass, and they know what is yet to come.
He knows little, or he knows much;
he knows the past.
He knows the present;
he knows the modes of conduct of all sentient beings; he knows their course of practice.
He knows the element;
he knows arising;
he knows rebirth.

For example, O sons of the Victor, it is like a well-trained physician who has mastered the entire eightfold Ayurveda, who is skilled in all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and devoted to the application of all medicinal substances and instruments; he knows the constitution (*dhātu*) of sentient beings whose bodies are afflicted by various diseases,
and he knows their strength.
He knows the proper time;
he knows the medicine;

[he knows] diseases caused by wind, bile, phlegm, or a combination of all three; blood disorders, those born of undigested matter (*āmaja*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), dropsy (*jalodara*), heart disease, leprosy, itching, ringworm, pustules and the like, and poisons such as erysipelas and so forth.

He knows; having known everything, he employs various kinds of medicinal substances through the application of emetics, purgatives, powder-formulations, nasal therapies (*nasya*), bloodletting, bandaging, ghee, oil, and child-powder formulations— by means of digestive, emetic, and therapeutic applications—
he pacifies all those diseases of all sentient beings.
They shall be liberated from various diseases and from the fears of various diseases.

In the very same way, O sons of the Conqueror, the Tathāgata—endowed with various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the divine eye, the divine ear, and so forth, and possessed of the eightfold Ayurveda; skilled in the application of various elements (*dhātu*) and dispositions (*āśaya*)—is worthy of liberating those beings who are afflicted by the diseases of passion, hatred, and delusion, as well as the diseases of the primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa* and *upakleśa*); those who are shrouded by pride, intoxication, and arrogance; and those who are enveloped by desire, grief, fear, and anger, for the sake of their deliverance from the realms of hell, the animal womb, and the world of Yama.
By means of various skillful methods, various types of applications, and various playful displays of meditative concentration and supernatural powers, he liberates sentient beings;
having established them in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, he causes them to attain final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
They shall be completely liberated from unwholesome states.
He establishes them in the noble eightfold path.

Just as, sons of good family, the orb of the moon, endowed with skill in means, for the sake of sentient beings who are to be disciplined by the roots of goodness of their respective elements, shows itself as having disappeared and displays the form of a half-moon orb.
He demonstrates the dark fortnights and the bright fortnights;
he displays the full orb of the moon;
he dispels all blinding darkness.
It refreshes all the grasses, forests, shrubs, medicinal herbs, fruits, and so forth.

In the very same way, O sons of the Conqueror, the Tathāgatas display the skill in the practice of the path and the attainment of final nirvāṇa for sentient beings who are shrouded by various sufferings and who are to be disciplined according to their various dispositions; they likewise display birth.
He displays the sovereignty of a universal monarch;
he displays the delights of play, women, laughter, dance, perfumes, garlands, and amorous pastimes;
[he displays the renunciation of the household, the going forth into homelessness, and the practice of austerities].
He displays the subduing of Māra’s forces and the turning of the wheel of Dharma; he demonstrates the satisfying of all sentient beings by raining down the great cloud of Dharma.

Even though the Tathāgatas have entered parinirvāṇa, it is solely through acts such as honoring their various spheres of activity, the construction of stūpas and monasteries, the fashioning of images and statues, the offering of robes, the going forth, the renunciation, the honoring of the community of monks, and the writing, reciting, and reading of the Vinaya and Dharma that [they continue to manifest].
They liberate all sentient beings. Through their skill in means regarding the undertaking of training, retention, vows, observances, fasting, and restraint,
they liberate [all sentient beings] from all hells, animal births, the world of Yama, the inopportune states, and the miserable destinies, up to the point that they bring them complete refreshment.
By means of hearing the Dharma, they establish them in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Then, at that time, it occurred to some sons of the gods of limited intelligence:
"Does this Tathāgata wish to enter the realm of final nirvāṇa so soon? Having thought this, they became dejected.
...for this purpose, he describes and indicates his final nirvāṇa.
Having assembled a great assembly, he displays various miraculous transformations of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-vikurvāṇa-prātihārya*).

Just as the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas performed the work of a Tathāgata by sustaining a very long life for the sake of all sentient beings, [he likewise acts] to deliver them from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
"Thinking, 'In this way, by means of this, all the tasks of a Tathāgata have not yet been completed by this Tathāgata;
therefore, he praises the transcendence of sorrow,' they became silent.
Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, knowing the thoughts of those sons of the gods with his own mind, spoke thus to those sons of the gods:"
“O sons of gods, do not think thus; do not speak thus;
do not be despondent in mind.

The Tathāgatas, through many roots of merit—such as skill in means, various means, wisdom, meditative concentrations, and so forth—and through the power of their vows, teach the Dharma to sentient beings of diverse dispositions.”
O sons of the gods, just as I have seen the display of miraculous transformations through the skillful means of former Tathāgatas, so do I know this.
It is not that the Tathāgata wishes to reveal or to perform something extraordinary—the Great King of Sūtras called the "Miracle of the Empowerment of the Buddha-Forces.
Furthermore, O sons of the gods, the Tathāgatas do not pass into final nirvāṇa.
The parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas does not exist;
there is no exhaustion of their lifespan.
For immeasurable millions of eons, and for inexpressible kalpas, the Tathāgatas remain.
Moreover, through skillful means, they manifest the final nirvana of sentient beings;
yet no coming or going exists for the Tathāgatas.
They likewise manifest the disappearance of the true Dharma.

In whatever way he perceives beings who are to be disciplined through parinirvāṇa, those to be disciplined by means of the [Dharma-]elements, or those of a turbid nature—who lack faith in the Tathāgata and fail to show respect or obedience—the Tathāgata accordingly manifests parinirvāṇa; yet, no coming or going exists for the Tathāgatas. All sentient beings then become matured in their roots of virtue.
Those who long for a vision of the Tathāgata, who are worthy of worship, and who desire to hear the Dharma—
just as the lunar disk shines, so do the Tathāgatas arise in the world for the benefit of many people and for the happiness of many people,
for the purpose of illuminating and manifesting the Three Jewels among gods and humans; yet, no birth of the Tathāgatas exists.

Sons of good family, it is just as if various forms were seen in a well-polished mirror-surface, yet no visible object exists there; neither the arrival nor the departure of the reflection is perceived.
In the same way, sons of gods, the body of the Tathāgata is to be viewed.

Sons of good family, it is just as if a well-trained magician, having displayed various cities, gateways, gardens, various chariots, the form of a universal monarch, and various pleasures and games, were then to make them vanish.
Neither its departure nor its arrival is seen; in this very way, the appearance and the final nirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas are to be viewed.

Furthermore, O sons of the gods, by virtue of their former vows, the Tathāgatas—though they have entered final nirvāṇa, though they have been in final nirvāṇa for an eon, or even though they have been in final nirvāṇa for ten million eons—[are present] for the honoring and reverencing of sentient beings, for the construction of reliquaries and stūpas, for the making of images, for the grasping of their names, and for the upholding and honoring of the True Dharma.

Even those situated in various world-systems liberate [beings] from all hells, animal births, the world of Yama, the inopportune states, the miserable destinies, and the fallen states, as well as from all sufferings, until they gradually awaken to unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What need is there to mention those who will worship the Tathāgatas with direct offerings of perfumes, flowers, garlands, ointments, garments, and ornaments?

And those sons of gods, whatever beings, who for hundreds of thousands of years or millions of kalpas after the final nirvāṇa, with palms joined together, shall once utter the name, saying "Homage to the Buddha," and cast a flower into the sky—they shall all bring an end to suffering.

Let alone the flower cast into the sky; whatever beings, following that example, for the sake of honoring the Tathāgata, shall uphold even a single precept of the Tathāgata for one day, one night, or one muhūrta, being intent upon the thought of worshipping the Tathāgata—[they shall all bring an end to suffering].
Having brought an end to all suffering, they will gradually realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
